items.title: Kodak invented the digital camera in 1975
items.claim: Steven Sasson, a Kodak engineer, built the first digital camera prototype in 1975. What happened to it?

options.text: Kodak rushed it to market and dominated the digital camera industry
Kodak management, worried about cannibalising film sales, suppressed the project; the company filed for bankruptcy in 2012 having failed the digital transition
It was stolen by a competitor before it could be developed

items.reveal:
Sasson's prototype was a 3.6 kg device using a CCD sensor and a cassette tape, taking 23 seconds to capture a 0.01 megapixel black-and-white image. He filed a patent in 1978.

Kodak's response, as Sasson later recalled, was 'that's cute, but don't tell anyone about it.' Film and processing had 60-70% gross margins. Kodak did launch digital products from the 1990s but couldn't restructure around a business model with lower margins.

The company filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in January 2012.
items.why: Owning the future technology isn't enough — you have to be willing to destroy your current revenue. Few large organisations can.

items.title: Quality assurance and quality control are different things
items.claim: A car plant inspects every vehicle at the end of the line and rejects defective units. Which approach is this?

options.text: Quality assurance, because it ensures quality
Quality control — defect detection after the fact. Quality assurance builds quality into the process so defects don't arise

items.reveal:
W. Edwards Deming, who worked in postwar Japan, argued that inspecting defects out is more expensive than preventing them. His '14 Points' for management (1986) included 'cease dependence on inspection to achieve quality'.

Toyota's andon-cord system stops the line whenever a worker sees a problem — quality is built upstream. Quality control still happens, but as a back-stop, not the main mechanism. ISO 9001 audits processes (assurance), not products (control).
items.why: Two firms with identical defect rates can have very different cost structures depending on whether defects are prevented or caught.

items.title: Quick ratio strips out the inventory you can't sell fast
items.claim: A retailer has current assets of £600,000 (including £400,000 inventory) and current liabilities of £300,000. What is the quick (acid-test) ratio?
items.reveal:
Quick ratio = (current assets - inventory) / current liabilities = (£600,000 - £400,000) / £300,000 = 0.67. Current ratio would be 2.0 — looking healthy. The acid-test reveals the firm could not cover short-term liabilities without selling stock.

The rule of thumb that quick ratio should exceed 1.0 is industry-dependent. Supermarkets routinely operate below 0.5 because they sell stock for cash before paying suppliers.
items.why: Two firms with identical current ratios can have very different real liquidity. Inventory turnover matters as much as the ratio number.
